parts.title: Inflammation in mothers and babies, and how it relates to children's weight and body size in the first year of life when mothers have diabetes that starts in pregnancy: the MySweetheart study
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Background

Gestational diabetes is a type of diabetes that starts during pregnancy. It often comes with a low, long-lasting level of inflammation, which is the body's natural response to injury or stress. We still do not know whether this inflamed environment affects how big and heavy children are in early childhood. In this study, we looked at women who had gestational diabetes and measured inflammation in two places: in the mother's blood, and in the baby's blood from the umbilical cord. We then checked whether these measurements were linked to the children's weight and body mass index (BMI, a measure of weight compared with height) up to 1 year old.

Methods

This study is a follow-up analysis of the MySweetheart study, which followed women and their babies over time. We included 193 women with gestational diabetes and their children. We measured three inflammation markers in the mother's blood at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy, and in the baby's cord blood: CRP, IL-6 and TNF-α. These are proteins that the body makes when it is inflamed. For the children, we looked at whether they were small or large for their pregnancy length at birth, their weight, and their BMI at birth and at 1 year. We took into account the child's sex and age. We used two kinds of statistical models: one that looks at one marker at a time, and one that looks at several markers together. In all of them, we took into account the mother's BMI before pregnancy, her age and her ethnic background.

Results

The mothers were 33.6 ± 4.8 years old on average, and their BMI before pregnancy was 25.9 ± 5.6 kg/m2. (The number after ± shows how much the values typically spread around the average.) On average, they had their first visit for gestational diabetes at 29 ± 2.4 weeks of pregnancy. They gave birth at 39.7 ± 1.1 weeks, and the babies weighed 3.4 ± 0.46 kg on average. Of the babies, 11.8% were large for their pregnancy length and 10.8% were small. At 1 year old, the children weighed 9.8 ± 1.2 kg on average, and their BMI z-score was 0.23 ± 1.1 kg/m2. A z-score shows how far a child's value is above or below the average for children of the same age.

When we looked at the mother's markers alone, higher TNF-α at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy was linked to babies being small for their pregnancy length, and to lower weight and BMI at birth and at 1 year (p ≤ 0.034). A p-value tells us how often a link this strong would turn up by chance alone if there were really no link at all. When we looked at the baby's markers alone, and when we looked at both together, higher CRP in the cord blood was linked to a lower BMI at 1 year (p ≤ 0.020).

Conclusions

In women with gestational diabetes, inflammation markers in the mother and in the baby each had their own influence on the children's size and weight during the first year of life. This held true regardless of the mother's age, her BMI before pregnancy and her ethnic background. These results suggest that low-level inflammation during pregnancy may affect the growing baby by lowering its weight and BMI. They may also help shape future plans for checking on women with gestational diabetes and their children, tailored to each family.

Keywords: gestational diabetes, children's size and weight, inflammation around the time of birth, CRP in cord blood, inflammation-promoting proteins in the mother
parts.introduction_first:
Inflammation is the body's natural response to injury or stress. When it stays high, it is linked to a greater risk of several health problems. These include insulin resistance, where the body stops responding properly to insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar. They also include high blood sugar, metabolic syndrome (a group of problems such as high blood sugar, high blood pressure and extra belly fat that tend to appear together), and heart and blood vessel disease (1–3).

More inflammation during pregnancy raises the risk of short-term problems for both the mother and the baby. These include miscarriage, gestational diabetes (diabetes that starts in pregnancy), preeclampsia (high blood pressure in pregnancy), early birth, babies who grow too slowly in the womb, and birth defects (4–8). Researchers have also recently pointed to long-term problems in children, such as certain behaviour problems and mental health disorders (9).

In women with gestational diabetes, the body may be in a state of long-lasting, low-level inflammation, and this often starts before the diabetes is diagnosed (10). The link between gestational diabetes and inflammation is complicated. Some studies have found higher levels of inflammation-promoting proteins in the blood of women with gestational diabetes and in their babies' umbilical cord blood. These proteins include C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and/or IL-1a. However, not all studies have found this (11–16).
parts.introduction_rest:
As far as we know, no one has yet studied whether inflammation markers in the mother's blood during pregnancy are linked to a child's weight or BMI in the first year of life when the mother has gestational diabetes. Most studies in the general population have found the opposite of what you might expect. Women with higher levels of inflammation-promoting proteins during pregnancy tended to have babies who were lighter and less fatty at birth (17–21). This was also true in the HAPO study (short for Hyperglycemia and Adverse Pregnancy Outcome), a large study that included women with many different levels of blood sugar during pregnancy. In one study of pregnant women in general, however, this link was not statistically significant (22). This means that study could not show a link, though it does not prove there is none.

The link has also been looked at after birth. In healthy pregnancies, the level of CRP in the mother's blood at 20 to 28 weeks of pregnancy (the second third of pregnancy) has been linked to more body fat in childhood. It has also been linked to more fat around the trunk, such as the belly, in children aged 3 to 5 (23).

Researchers have also looked at the baby's own blood. Studies in different groups of people, both pregnant women in general and groups where many women have gestational diabetes, found no link between inflammation markers in cord blood and the baby's weight and body fat at birth. These markers included CRP, IL-6 and TNF-α (18, 24–26). However, no one has studied whether inflammation markers in the mother's blood or in the baby's cord blood, including CRP, IL-6 and TNF-α, are linked to children's size and weight in women with gestational diabetes (18, 21). We also know little about how these markers affect children in the first year of life after birth in this group.

Obesity and ageing are both linked to low-level inflammation (27–29). Inflammation markers also differ between ethnic groups. This shows how genes, surroundings and social factors work together in complicated ways to create differences in health between groups of people (30). A recent study in the general population found that inflammation linked to obesity in the mother during pregnancy raised the risk of obesity in childhood, and that this effect depended on the ethnic group (31). Still, it is unclear whether this low-level inflammation during pregnancy in women with gestational diabetes affects how big and heavy their children are. It is also unclear whether it helps cause problems with the body's use of sugar and fat in children, both in early childhood and later in life.

In this study, we had two aims. First, we wanted to find out whether inflammation markers in the mother and in the baby are linked to the children's size and weight at birth and at 1 year, in a group of women with gestational diabetes. Second, we wanted to find out whether these links hold true regardless of the mother's BMI before pregnancy, her age and her ethnic background.
parts.methods:
## 2. Materials and methods

### 2.1. How the study was set up, and how women agreed to take part

This study is a follow-up analysis of the MySweetheart trial. That trial was a randomised controlled trial, which means women were split by chance into two groups, and the groups were then compared. It included 211 women aged 18 or older who had gestational diabetes, together with their babies (Clinicaltrials.gov NCT02890693) (32). The women were followed from pregnancy until one year after giving birth, in the Diabetes and Pregnancy Unit at Lausanne University Hospital in Switzerland.

Women were diagnosed with gestational diabetes between 24 and 32 weeks of pregnancy, using the rules of the International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) (33). We have described the trial's plan in detail before (32). We left out women who had to stay strictly in bed, women with a severe mental health disorder, women who already had diabetes, and women who did not understand English or French. Every woman who took part signed a consent form after being told what the study involved. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki, a set of ethical rules for research with people, and the standards of good clinical practice. The Human Research Ethics Committee of the Canton de Vaud approved the plan (study number 2016-00745). After their first visit and after signing the consent form, women were placed by chance into one of two groups: usual care or the intervention group.

### 2.2. The two groups

#### 2.2.1. Usual care group

Women in the usual care group were treated following the guidelines of the American Diabetes Association and the Endocrine Society for managing gestational diabetes (34, 35). After their diagnosis, they had regular appointments every 1 to 3 weeks with a doctor or a nurse who specialises in diabetes, and with a dietitian. They were encouraged to be more physically active (34).

At their first visit, between 24 and 32 weeks of pregnancy, they learned how to check their own blood sugar. They did this 4 times a day: once in the morning before eating, and 2 hours after each meal. If their blood sugar stayed above the targets two or more times over 1 to 2 weeks, despite changes to their lifestyle, they were given treatment to lower it. This was insulin, or very rarely metformin, a medicine that helps control blood sugar. The choice depended on the woman's blood sugar readings and her preferences. The targets were a fasting blood sugar above 5.3 mmol/l, a blood sugar 1 hour after a meal above 8 mmol/l, and/or a blood sugar 2 hours after a meal above 7 mmol/l.

After giving birth, the blood sugar checks and the treatment to lower blood sugar were stopped. At the 6 to 8 week visit after birth, women saw a doctor and a dietitian after an oral glucose tolerance test (a test of how the body handles a sugary drink) to discuss how to manage things next.

#### 2.2.2. Intervention group

Women in the intervention group received usual care plus a lifestyle and psychosocial programme. It was run by several kinds of specialists working together. It focused on how women ate, eating a balanced diet, physical activity and breastfeeding. It also included support for mental health, with depression being checked for and treated during and after pregnancy. During pregnancy and for up to 1 year after birth, each woman had a lifestyle coach to support her (see (32) for more details).

### 2.3. What we measured and when

For this analysis, we used information about the mothers from their first visit for gestational diabetes, at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy. We used information about the babies at birth and at 1 year.

At the first visit, we collected details about each woman's background, such as her age, ethnic background and whether she had given birth before. We also measured her body size and took blood to measure inflammation markers in the serum, the liquid part of the blood. Right after birth, we took blood from the umbilical cord to measure inflammation markers. The babies' body measurements at birth came from the hospital birth record. At 1 year after birth, we collected the children's body measurements, including weight and length.

### 2.4. What we measured in mothers, babies in the womb and children

#### 2.4.1. Background details and other factors about the mothers

At the first visit for gestational diabetes, we collected details about each woman's background, including her age, ethnic background and whether she had given birth before. We sorted ethnic background into two groups: Low risk (Europe, North America) and High metabolic risk (Asia, Central and South America, Africa, Oceania) (35).

We worked out each woman's BMI before pregnancy from her weight in the medical records and her height, measured at the first visit at the diabetes clinic. In rare cases where the weight before pregnancy was not written in the records, the woman told us it herself at the first visit. We measured height at the first visit to the nearest 0.1 cm, using a Seca® height scale that was regularly checked. We worked out how much weight each woman gained during pregnancy by subtracting her weight before pregnancy from her weight at the end of pregnancy.

We sorted the medical treatment to lower blood sugar into two groups: no treatment, and treatment with insulin and/or, very rarely, metformin. We also measured HbA1c, a measure of average blood sugar over the past few months. We used a chemical test that uses light (a method called conjugation with boronate; Afinion®).

#### 2.4.2. Inflammation markers in the mothers and in the babies in the womb (cord blood)

At the visit at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy, we measured three inflammation markers in the mother's serum: CRP, IL-6 and TNF-α. At birth, we measured the same three markers again in the cord blood, taken from the umbilical artery (36).

CRP was measured at Lausanne University Hospital in small samples of serum. The test used latex particles to make the CRP show up as a cloudiness, which a machine then measured (a latex-enhanced immunoturbidimetric assay on a Cobas 8000 autoanalyzer, Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany). The test worked as the maker described. We also measured IL-6 (U-PLEX Human IL-6 Antibody Set) and TNF-α (U-PLEX Human TNF-α Antibody Set) using ELISA, a test that uses antibodies to detect a particular protein, following the maker's instructions.

#### 2.4.3. Background details and results for the children

At birth, we recorded each baby's weight (in grams) and length (in centimetres). We then turned these into percentiles and z-scores using the Intergrowth 21st newborn size application tool (37). A percentile shows what share of babies are smaller than a given baby. A z-score shows how far a baby's value is above or below the average for babies of the same sex and pregnancy length. We also worked out each baby's BMI.

We counted a baby as large for their pregnancy length if their birth weight was above the 90th percentile, and as small for their pregnancy length if it was below the 10th percentile, for their sex and pregnancy length. We worked out the length of pregnancy from the date of the last period. When the length of pregnancy had been adjusted during an early scan in the womb, we used the adjusted date. The babies' body measurements at birth came from the medical records. If a baby was born in another hospital or clinic, that hospital or clinic gave us the measurements.

At the 1 year visit, we measured each child's weight (in kilograms) and length (in centimetres) using standard methods (38), and we worked out their BMI. We calculated z-scores for weight, length and BMI using the WHO Anthro Survey Analyser tool, offline version (39).

#### 2.4.4. What we used to explain the results, and what we measured as results

The possible explaining factors were the inflammation markers in the mother (at the first visit for gestational diabetes) and in the baby in the womb (in cord blood): CRP, IL-6 and TNF-α. The results we looked at were the children's body measurements at birth and at 1 year. At birth, these were weight, BMI, being large for their pregnancy length and being small for their pregnancy length. At 1 year, they were weight and BMI.

### 2.5. How we analysed the data

We analysed the data with the statistics program Stata/SE 16.0 (StataCorp LLC, TX, USA). First, we checked whether each measurement followed a normal distribution, the familiar bell-shaped pattern where most values sit near the middle. We did this with histograms (bar charts of how often each value appears) and Q-Q plots (graphs that show whether data match a bell shape). The results we were trying to explain did follow a normal distribution.

We described measurements that can take any value as averages with standard deviations, which show how spread out the values are. For yes-or-no results, we gave the number of people and the percentage (Table 1). To compare the two groups, we used the unpaired t-test for measurements that followed a normal distribution, the Mann-Whitney test for measurements that did not, and Fisher's exact test for yes-or-no results.

In all analyses, the explaining factors and the results did not differ between the two groups (intervention versus usual care), and the size of the differences was similar. So we combined the women from both groups and took into account which group each woman was in, in every analysis. Where it made sense, we also took into account the child's age and sex.

We used a Spearman's rank correlation test to check whether the mothers' and babies' inflammation markers rose and fell together, and whether any two markers were so closely linked that they would carry almost the same information (Supplementary Table 1). Next, we looked at each marker on its own, using linear regression for measurements and logistic regression for yes-or-no results (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). These are statistical models that estimate how much a result changes as a marker goes up. We then took the markers from the mother and from the baby in the womb that had a p-value below 0.05 in this one-marker-at-a-time analysis and put them into stepwise multiple regression models. In these models, markers are added or removed one at a time to find the best combination.

We built three models, each looking at several markers together. The first used only the mother's markers, the second used only the babies' markers, and the third used both. We had babies' markers for 39 women. We also took into account the mother's age, BMI before pregnancy and ethnic background, as well as the group each woman was in, the child's age and sex.

We did this to find the most significant markers from the mother and from the baby in the womb for the children's body measurements at birth and at 1 year. We also wanted to see how much these markers mattered on their own, apart from the mother's age, ethnic background and obesity, which are known to be linked to low-level inflammation (27–29) (Table 2).

For every analysis, we report the size of each link as a β-coefficient for measurements and as an adjusted odds ratio for yes-or-no results. An adjusted odds ratio shows how the odds of a yes-or-no result change as a marker goes up, after taking the other factors into account. For each one, we also give a 95% confidence interval, a range that shows how precise the estimate is. We called a result statistically significant when its p-value was below 0.05.

parts.results:
## 3. Results

We started with 211 women who had gestational diabetes. As we described in an earlier paper (38), we left one woman out because her diabetes was diagnosed too early, before 13 weeks of pregnancy. We also left out 17 women, either because they were carrying more than one baby, because their babies were born early (before 37 weeks of pregnancy), or both. That left 193 women and their children in our analyses.

### 3.1. The mothers, the babies at birth and the children at 1 year

Table 1 describes the mothers, the inflammation markers in the babies' cord blood, and the children's size and weight at birth and at 1 year.

On average, the mothers were 33.6 ± 4.8 years old, and their BMI before pregnancy was 25.9 ± 5.6 kg/m2. They had their first visit for gestational diabetes at 29 ± 2.4 weeks of pregnancy, which falls within the 24 to 32 weeks when this visit is usually made. They gave birth at 39.7 ± 1.1 weeks, and the babies weighed 3.4 ± 0.46 kg on average. Of the babies, 11.8% were large for their pregnancy length and 10.8% were small for their pregnancy length. At 1 year old, the children weighed 9.8 ± 1.2 kg on average, and their BMI z-score was 0.23 ± 1.1 kg/m2.

We also checked whether the inflammation markers in the mother's blood and in the baby's cord blood tended to rise and fall together. They did not: the links between them were not statistically significant (Supplementary Table 1).

### 3.2. Links between the mothers' and babies' markers and the children's size and weight at birth and at 1 year, looking at one marker at a time

#### 3.2.1. At birth

When we looked at one marker at a time, higher TNF-α in the mother's blood at her first visit for gestational diabetes was linked to lower weight and BMI in the baby at birth. It was also linked to a higher chance of the baby being small for their pregnancy length.

To describe these links, we use a few terms. A β-coefficient is a number that shows how much a child's measurement changes, on average, for each step up in a marker. A minus sign means the measurement goes down as the marker goes up. A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that fits well with our data. For the chance of being small, we use an odds ratio (OR). An odds ratio above 1 means a higher chance, and one below 1 means a lower chance.

For TNF-α, the β-coefficient was -0.107 (CI: -0.189 to -0.026) for weight and -0.501 (CI: -0.816 to -0.186) for BMI, with p-values of 0.010 and 0.002. For the chance of being small, the odds ratio was 0.492 (CI: 0.056 to 0.927), with p = 0.027.

Higher CRP in the cord blood was also linked to lower weight and BMI at birth. Its β-coefficient was -0.370 (CI: -0.659 to -0.081) for weight, with p = 0.015, and -1.052 (CI: -1.900 to -0.205) for BMI, with p = 0.017.

We found no link between the mothers' or babies' inflammation markers and babies being large for their pregnancy length (all p-values were 0.199 or higher, Supplementary Table 2).

#### 3.2.2. At 1 year

At 1 year, TNF-α in the mother's blood at her first visit for gestational diabetes was again linked to lower weight and BMI in the child. The β-coefficient was -0.376 (CI: -0.625 to -0.128) for weight, with p = 0.003, and -0.641 (CI: -1.003 to -0.279) for BMI, with p = 0.001.

The cord blood markers were also linked to a lower BMI at 1 year. For CRP, the β-coefficient was -2.566 (CI: -3.666 to -1.465), with p = 0.000. For TNF-α, it was -2.177 (CI: -3.671 to -0.684), with p = 0.006 (Supplementary Table 3).

### 3.3. Links between the mothers' and babies' markers and the children's size and weight at birth and at 1 year, looking at several markers together

Table 2 shows the statistically significant results from all of our analyses that looked at several markers together.

#### 3.3.1. At birth

In the models that used only the mothers' markers, TNF-α at the first visit for gestational diabetes was linked to lower weight and BMI in the baby. The β-coefficient was -0.090 (CI: -0.170 to -0.010) for weight, with p = 0.028, and -0.455 (CI: -0.773 to -0.137) for BMI, with p = 0.005. It was also linked to a higher chance of the baby being small for their pregnancy length, with an odds ratio of 1.609 (CI: 1.036 to 2.500), with p = 0.034.

We found no statistically significant links between the mothers' or babies' inflammation markers and the children's size and weight in the models that used only the babies' markers, or in the model that used both together (all p-values were 0.05 or higher).

#### 3.3.2. At 1 year

In the models that used the mothers' markers, TNF-α at the first visit for gestational diabetes was linked to lower weight and BMI in the child at 1 year. The β-coefficient was -0.411 (CI: -0.659 to -0.163) for weight, with p = 0.001, and -0.702 (CI: -1.069 to -0.335) for BMI, with p = 0.000.

In the models that used the babies' markers, and in the model that used both together, higher CRP in the cord blood was linked to a lower BMI at 1 year. The β-coefficient was -2.838 (CI: -4.029 to -1.646), with p = 0.001.
parts.discussion:
## 4. Discussion

This study is a follow-up analysis of the MySweetheart study, which followed women with gestational diabetes and their children over time. We looked ahead in time, rather than looking back at records that had already been collected. We found that inflammation markers in the mother and in the baby predicted the children's weight and BMI during the first year of life. This held true regardless of the mother's age, her BMI before pregnancy and her ethnic background.

When we took the other factors into account, higher TNF-α in the mother's blood at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy was linked to babies being small for their pregnancy length. It was also linked to lower weight and BMI at birth and at 1 year. CRP in the cord blood, on the other hand, was linked to a lower BMI at 1 year, even after we took the mother's factors into account. So the mother's inflammation-promoting proteins predicted lower weight and BMI both at birth and up to 1 year, while the effect of the baby's CRP showed up at 1 year.

### 4.1 How inflammation in mothers and babies relates to children's size and weight at birth

In our study, women with higher TNF-α in their blood at their first visit for gestational diabetes, at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy, had babies with lower weight and BMI at birth. These babies were also more likely to be small for their pregnancy length. This matches a recent study in a healthy population, which found that higher levels of inflammation markers such as CRP and IL-6 went together with lower birth weight (17).

Other studies have looked at how inflammation in mothers relates to babies' birth results. Some studied healthy pregnant women, and others studied women whose bodies had some trouble handling sugar (19, 20, 22, 40, 41). In the general population, CRP in the mother's blood early in pregnancy was linked to more babies being small for their pregnancy length (40). In the third trimester, the last three months of pregnancy, CRP was linked to lower weight and a smaller sum of skinfolds at birth. Skinfolds are thin layers of fat under the skin, and adding them up gives a rough measure of body fat. This was true both in the general population and in a group of women from the HAPO Study, a large international study of blood sugar in pregnancy (19, 20).

Not every study agrees. In a healthy group of pregnant women without gestational diabetes, TNF-α and IL-6 in the third trimester were not linked to the baby's body fat or birth weight (22). In a study that included women both with and without gestational diabetes, IL-6 in the second and third trimesters was linked to lower weight and a smaller sum of skinfolds at birth (41). Another study looked at women who had already had a very large baby, but who did not have gestational diabetes. It found no link between the mother's IL-6 and TNF-α and the baby's birth weight or body fat, either for all babies together or for boys alone. However, in girls, higher IL-6 in the mother's third trimester was linked to a smaller sum of skinfolds at birth (18).

So most earlier studies have found that higher levels of the mother's inflammation-promoting markers, including CRP, IL-6 and/or TNF-α, go together with smaller size and weight at birth. Our data are the first to show this in a group of women at high risk for problems with their metabolism, the way the body uses energy, because they have gestational diabetes.

There is evidence that the link between a baby's size at birth and heart and metabolic disease later in life follows a U-shaped curve. This means that babies who are too small and babies who are too large both have a higher risk, while babies of a normal size have the lowest risk. It shows how important it is for a baby to grow at the right pace for good health later on (42, 43).

The mother's inflammation-promoting proteins may affect the baby's growth in the womb in direct and indirect ways. They may act on how the placenta develops, works and controls the immune system. The placenta is the organ that feeds the baby in the womb. The proteins may also affect how hormones are made and work in the mother and baby together (41, 44, 45). In our study, IL-6 was not linked to BMI or weight. This may be because IL-6 is more closely tied to fat stored around the belly (46), which we did not measure directly.

We found no links between inflammation markers in the cord blood and the children's size and weight at birth. Other studies have found the same. These included studies in the general population and in groups where many women had gestational diabetes, diabetes before pregnancy, or both. They found no link between cord blood IL-6, CRP, or higher CRP (CRP above 0.3 mg/l, which is 2.9 nmol/l) and one or more measures of size, body fat or both at birth. These measures included weight, weight z-score, being large for their pregnancy length, fat mass, the percentage of body fat, and the sum of skinfold thickness (21, 24–26).

During birth, the levels of inflammation-promoting markers in cord blood naturally rise. Other things may also affect this rise, such as how long the labour lasts and whether the baby is born by natural birth or by caesarean section (47, 48). So cord blood inflammation markers may reflect a mix of the baby's inflammation before birth and around the time of birth. This could explain why these markers were linked to the children's size and weight later in life, at 1 year, but not at birth.

Yeung and colleagues found a link between cord blood CRP and DNA methylation in the cord blood (49). DNA methylation is a chemical tag that can switch genes on or off without changing the genes themselves. The tags were found especially in parts of genes involved in building new blood vessels and in inflammation, and these could in turn affect the risk of heart and metabolic disease later on. Recent research suggests that methylation in certain inflammation-related genes in cord blood is linked to measures of body fat later in development, such as in early childhood (50). More research is needed to understand the complicated ways in which inflammation-promoting proteins in cord blood may affect children's body make-up and metabolism during childhood.

### 4.2 How metabolism in mothers and babies relates to children's weight and BMI in childhood

In our group, women with higher TNF-α in their blood during the third trimester had children with lower weight and BMI at 1 year. This agrees with a study of women in which only a small share (4.5%) had gestational diabetes. In that study, higher CRP in the second trimester was linked to a higher fat mass index in childhood. The fat mass index is a measure of how much fat a child carries compared with their size. It was also higher in the trunk, the middle part of the body. However, this showed up later in development, in early childhood (3 to 5 years) and middle childhood (7 to 10 years) (23).

Our results do not agree with a study in the general population. There, IL-6 and TNF-α in the first trimester were not linked to measures of body fat in children aged 2 to 6 years, including weight and BMI z-scores (31). In another study, IL-6 and TNF-α in the first trimester were not linked to weight and body fat at 6 months of age, either for all babies together or for boys alone. In girls, however, they were linked to measures of body fat (18). In a large study of the general population in Denmark, CRP, TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-1b in the third trimester were not linked to children's BMI, waist size, blood pressure, blood sugar handling or blood fat levels at the age of 20 years (51).

There is little information on how inflammation in the baby, measured in cord blood, relates to growth during the first years of life. The study of women who had already had a very large baby, without gestational diabetes, found no link between cord blood IL-6 and TNF-α and the children's weight or body fat at 6 months (18). As for the baby's own markers, a study of children born extremely early, before 28 weeks of pregnancy, found that higher IL-6 in the newborn on day 1 was linked to a higher risk of obesity at 2 years. This held when several factors were taken into account at the same time (52).

### 4.3 Ideas about how metabolism in mothers and babies might affect children's size and weight in the first years of life when mothers have gestational diabetes

In pregnancies with gestational diabetes, the effects on children's size and weight come from many directions. They involve complicated processes in the mother, the placenta and the baby (38, 53, 54). These include the mother's insulin resistance, higher levels of inflammation-promoting proteins, and the effects these have on how the placenta works (41, 44). Inflammation and high blood sugar upset the balance of insulin-like growth factors and adiponectin. These are hormones that help control growth and fat, and this can change how the baby grows and how its fat tissue develops (55, 56).

Exposure to gestational diabetes may also cause epigenetic changes. These are chemical tags on genes that change how genes are used without changing the genes themselves. Such changes can affect genes linked to the baby's development and could be one way that problems with metabolism appear later in life (57). On top of this, the mother's obesity and too much weight gain during pregnancy, which are common in women with gestational diabetes, each add to the risk of problems for the child (58, 59). Together, these factors show how complicated the picture is. To find possible targets for treatment, we need a full understanding of both inflammation and metabolism.

### 4.4 Strengths and limitations

As far as we know, this is the first study to look at how inflammation markers in mothers and babies affect children's size and weight at birth and up to 1 year of life in a group of women with gestational diabetes and their children, who are at high risk for problems with their metabolism. Another strength of our study is that we followed the women and their children over time.

Still, our study has some limitations. We measured the mother's inflammation markers only once during pregnancy. We did not include the children's height or head size, because we chose to focus on measures related to metabolic health. Because our aim was to study the link between inflammation markers and children's metabolic health in a group at high risk, we did not have a proper group of healthy people to compare with.

We had cord blood (from the umbilical artery) measurements for only 39 women. This could affect our results, especially the links we found. Because there were so few cord blood measurements, we could not analyse the women who received the study's treatment separately from those who received usual care, or separately by the baby's sex. However, the mothers' and babies' markers and the children's size and weight did not differ between these two groups. We also always took into account which group each woman was in.

### 4.5 Conclusions

Inflammation markers in the mother and in the baby each had their own influence on children's weight and BMI during the first year of life. These included TNF-α in the mother's blood at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy and CRP in the cord blood. This held true regardless of the mother's age, her ethnic background and her BMI before pregnancy. The effect of the baby's inflammation markers did not show up at birth, but it did at 1 year.

More research is needed to understand how the inflamed environment before and during birth might affect the growing baby. This may in turn help in designing ways to use inflammation markers in mothers and cord blood to lower the risk of problems with children's metabolism in the medium and long term.
